subjective.question: Why is alignment a key component of the action research model?
subjective.answer: Alignment refers to a characteristic of the relationship between two or more parts of a system. It represents the extent to which the features, operations, and characteristics of one system support the effectiveness of another system. A system's overall effectiveness is determined by the extent to which its different parts are aligned with each other; this alignment or fit concerns the relationships between inputs and transformations, between transformations and outputs, and among the subsystems of the transformation process. Changing any one part or feature of an organization often requires adjustments in the other parts to maintain an appropriate alignment. Thus, although quick fixes and change programs that focus on only one part of the organization may resolve some specific problems, they generally do not lead to complex organizational change or increase members' capacity to carry out change. Just as the teeth in two wheels of a watch must mesh perfectly for the watch to keep time, so do the parts of an organization need to mesh for it to be effective. The systemic perspective therefore suggests that diagnosis is the search for misfits among the various parts and subsystems of an organization.

subjective.question: "Measurement systems are methods of gathering, assessing, and disseminating information on the activities of groups and individuals in organizations." Discuss.
subjective.answer: Measurement systems are methods of gathering, assessing, and disseminating information on the activities of groups and individuals in organizations. Such data tell how well the organization is performing and are used to detect and control deviations from goals. Closely related to structural integration, measurement systems monitor organizational operations and feed data about work activities to managers and members so that they can better understand current performance and coordinate work. Effective information and control systems are clearly linked to strategic objectives; provide accurate, understandable and timely information; are accepted as legitimate by organization members; and produce benefits in excess of their cost.

subjective.question: Explain the purpose of diagnosis at the organizational level.
subjective.answer: The purpose of diagnosis at the organizational level is that the OD practitioner and client together analyze the data to identify problem areas and causal relationships. The diagnostic phase is used to determine the exact problem that needs solution, to identify the forces causing the situation, and to provide a basis for selecting effective change strategies and techniques. The practitioner and client may also agree to increase the range or depth of the available data by interview or questionnaire as a basis for further action programs.

subjective.question: What is the purpose of the gamesmanship mode of practitioner-client relationship?
subjective.answer: In the gamesmanship mode, members keep their true feelings about self-fulfillment and organizational effectiveness to themselves, under the assumption that sharing information may threaten personally desired outcomes. They make their own decisions about how to behave, thus taking responsibility for their behavior. This may include conforming outwardly to any decision-making procedure but manipulating strategic factors to gain personal goals. Members may favor change if they can see ways in which it can serve their personal interest.

subjective.question: Differentiate between an organization member and an OD practitioner.
subjective.answer: The organization member may be a manager, staff specialist, or some other key participant who is part of the client system, experiences the organization's problems directly, and owns and implements the change. The OD practitioner is the change agent — an OD professional from inside or outside the organization — who helps the client system diagnose its problems and plan and carry out improvement efforts. The member contributes knowledge of the system and responsibility for action, while the practitioner contributes OD expertise, process skills and, especially in the case of the external practitioner, objectivity.

subjective.question: Write down the disadvantages of the internal practitioner.
subjective.answer: The disadvantages of the internal practitioner are: (1) Lack of the specialized skills needed for organization development. (2) More likely to accept the organizational system as a given and accommodate their change tactics to the needs of management. (3) Other employees may not understand the practitioner's role and will certainly be influenced by his or her previous work and relationships in the organization. (4) May not have the necessary power and authority; internal practitioners are sometimes in a remote staff position and report to a mid-level manager.

subjective.question: Why is there no one best way of collecting data? Justify your answer.
subjective.answer: The third step in data collection is selecting a method of gathering data. There are many different types of data and many different methods of tapping data sources. There is no one best way to gather data — the selection of a method depends on the nature of the problem. Whatever method is adopted, data should be acquired in a systematic manner, thus allowing quantitative or qualitative comparison between elements of the system. The task in this step is to identify certain characteristics that may be measured to help in the achievement of the OD program objective and then to select an appropriate method to gather the required data.

subjective.question: What are the four possible modes of practitioner-client relationship? Discuss any one of them.
subjective.answer: The four possible modes of practitioner-client relationship are: (1) The apathetic mode: members keep their true ideas about self-fulfillment and organizational effectiveness to themselves, assuming that sharing this information will not make any difference. They follow established routines, take no responsibility for their actions, and simply do as they are told. (2) The gamesmanship mode: members keep their true feelings to themselves, assuming that sharing information may threaten personally desired outcomes; they conform outwardly but manipulate strategic factors to gain personal goals. (3) The charismatic mode: a limited number of members openly share ideas and feelings with the rest, based on perceptions of leadership; followers look for cues from their leaders, so responsibility is low for most members. (4) The consensus mode: members continuously share perceptions and feelings openly, both on self-fulfillment and organizational effectiveness. Personal viewpoints are seen as relevant to organization functioning and are expressed; decisions are made and differences are resolved through the sharing of viewpoints, and members see the OD process as consistent with their way of operating.

subjective.question: How can you differentiate task identity from task significance in the design components of diagnosis?
subjective.answer: Design components represent the way the organization positions and organizes itself within an environment (inputs) to achieve specific outputs, and they exist at three levels: organizational level, group level, and individual level. At the individual level, jobs have five key dimensions: skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, and feedback about results. Task identity measures the degree to which a job requires the completion of a relatively whole, identifiable piece of work. Skilled craftspeople, such as tool-and-die makers and carpenters, generally have jobs with high levels of task identity, because they are able to see a job through from beginning to end; assembly-line jobs involve only a limited piece of work and score low on task identity. Task significance identifies the degree to which a job has a significant impact on other people's lives. Custodial jobs in a hospital are likely to have more task significance than similar jobs in a toy factory, because hospital custodians are likely to see their jobs as affecting someone else's health and welfare.

subjective.question: Briefly describe the three steps of feedback in the action research model.
subjective.answer: Because action research is a collaborative activity, the diagnostic data are fed back to the client, usually in a group or work-team meeting. A feedback session generally has three steps. First, the consultant provides a summary of the data collected and some preliminary analysis. Next, there is a general discussion in which questions of clarification are raised and answered. Finally, some time is devoted to interpretation; at this stage some changes may be made in the consultant's analysis and interpretation. Thus, the consultant works collaboratively with the client to arrive at a final diagnosis that accurately describes the current state of the system.

subjective.question: Justify that outside data collection agents are more efficient than inside agents.
subjective.answer: Outside data-collection agents are more effective than internal personnel. The use of outside data-collection agents is recommended because it apparently makes respondents feel more secure and trusting that candid answers will not be used against them. There are also companies that develop data-collection instruments, test them and make them available commercially, so the instruments used are more reliable.

subjective.question: Describe the culture of an organization and its levels.
subjective.answer: Organization culture is the pattern of basic assumptions, values, norms, and artifacts shared by organization members. These shared meanings help members make sense out of everyday life in the organization. Organization culture includes four major elements existing at different levels of awareness: (1) Artifacts: the highest level of cultural manifestation; the visible symbols of the deeper levels of culture, including members' behaviors, clothing and language, and organizations' structure, systems, procedures and physical aspects. (2) Norms: just below the surface of cultural awareness are norms guiding how members should behave in a particular situation; these are unwritten rules of behavior, generally inferred by observing how members behave and interact with each other. (3) Values: the next deeper level includes values about what ought to be in organizations; values tell members what is important in the organization and what deserves their attention. (4) Basic assumptions: at the deepest level are the taken-for-granted assumptions about how organizational problems should be solved; they tell members how to perceive, think and feel about things, and are non-debatable.

subjective.question: Explain "feedback about results" as a design component at the individual level of diagnosis.
subjective.answer: Feedback about results involves the degree to which a job provides employees with direct and clear information about the effectiveness of task performance. Assembly-line jobs often provide high levels of feedback about results, whereas college professors must often contend with indirect and ambiguous feedback about how they are performing in the classroom.

subjective.question: Write down the disadvantages of external practitioners.
subjective.answer: The disadvantages of external practitioners are: (1) Outsiders are generally unfamiliar with the organization system and may not have sufficient knowledge of its technology, such as aerospace or chemistry. (2) They are unfamiliar with the culture, communication networks, and formal or informal power systems. (3) In some situations external practitioners may have difficulty gathering pertinent information simply because they are outsiders.

subjective.question: Explain entry into an OD relationship.
subjective.answer: Entry (problem identification) usually begins when a key executive in the organization, or someone with power and influence, senses that the organization has one or more problems that might be solved with the help of an OD practitioner. Contact between the consultant and client is what initiates the entry phase. After the contact, the consultant and the client begin the process of exploring with one another the possibilities of a working relationship. During this process, the consultant assesses: (a) the probability of relating with the client; (b) the motivation and values of the client; (c) the client's readiness for change; (d) the extent of resources available; and (e) potential leverage points of change.

subjective.question: Discuss "Open systems in organizations".
subjective.answer: Organizations are open systems: they exist in an environment, take inputs (human and other resources such as information, energy and materials) from it, transform those inputs through their internal processes and design components, and return outputs (products, services and member satisfaction) to the environment, with feedback informing the system about how well it is functioning. The parts of the system — inputs, transformations and outputs — must be aligned or fit together for the system to be effective, and diagnosis from an open-systems perspective searches for misfits among these parts and between the organization and its environment.

subjective.question: What are T-groups and process consultation in human process interventions? Discuss in detail.
subjective.answer: T-groups (training groups) are a laboratory training intervention in which a small, unstructured group of participants learns from its own interactions and evolving dynamics. There is no predetermined agenda; participants receive feedback from one another about their interpersonal behavior, communication and leadership, and learn how their actions affect others and how groups develop. Process consultation, associated with Edgar Schein, is an intervention in which the consultant helps the client to perceive, understand and act upon process events that occur in the client's environment — such as communication patterns, interpersonal relations, role behavior, decision-making and group dynamics — rather than solving the client's problem for them. The aim is to build the client's own diagnostic and problem-solving capability so that the client can continue to improve its processes after the consultant leaves.

subjective.question: What is the difference between an external and an internal consultant at the stage of diagnosis?
subjective.answer: At the diagnosis stage, the internal consultant is a member of the organization, so he or she already knows the organization's culture, technology, communication networks and power structure, and can gather data quickly through existing relationships; however, internal consultants may lack specialized diagnostic skills, may accept the system as a given, may be influenced by internal politics, and members may not give them candid information because of their known position. The external consultant, being an outsider, brings specialized diagnostic expertise and an objective, unbiased view, and members often trust that their candid answers will not be used against them; however, external consultants are unfamiliar with the organization's culture, technology and informal systems, and may face difficulty gathering pertinent information simply because they are outsiders.

subjective.question: Briefly explain the change activity within marginality.
subjective.answer: Marginality refers to the position of the OD practitioner who works at the boundary of the client system — connected to it but not fully captured by its norms, roles and politics. Change activity within marginality means using this in-between position productively: because the practitioner is not fully identified with any one group, he or she can remain comparatively objective and neutral, question taken-for-granted assumptions, move between groups (for example between management and employees), and mediate between them. This marginal position gives the practitioner freedom to introduce new ideas and facilitate change without being bound by the vested interests of any single part of the system.

subjective.question: Discuss skill variety as a major design component at the individual level of diagnosis.
subjective.answer: Skill variety is one of the five core job dimensions examined in individual-level diagnosis. It identifies the degree to which a job requires a range of activities and abilities to perform the work — that is, how many different skills and talents the job holder must use. Jobs high in skill variety are generally experienced as more challenging and meaningful, while jobs requiring only one narrow, repetitive activity score low on skill variety and tend to produce boredom and dissatisfaction.

subjective.question: What are the two features of the technological core that influence other design components of the organization? Discuss in detail.
subjective.answer: The technological core is the basic work activity of the organization — the way it converts inputs into outputs. Its two features that influence the other design components (structure, measurement systems, human resource systems and culture) are: (1) Task uncertainty — the extent to which the work is routine and predictable or variable and difficult to analyze. High uncertainty requires more flexible structures, richer communication and greater discretion for members, whereas routine technology fits mechanistic designs. (2) Task interdependence — the extent to which units and members depend on one another to complete their work (pooled, sequential or reciprocal). The greater the interdependence, the more coordination the organization needs through its structure, measurement and reward systems. Because the technological core shapes what coordination and control are possible, it powerfully influences how the other design components can be arranged.

subjective.question: "The term diagnosis is deceptive in its nature when applied to organizations." Discuss.
subjective.answer: The term diagnosis is borrowed from medicine, and it can mislead when applied to organizations. It suggests that the organization is a sick patient, that there is a single identifiable disease or problem, and that an expert doctor can examine it from outside and prescribe a cure. Organization development is different: diagnosis in OD is a collaborative process in which practitioner and client jointly collect and interpret data about how the system is functioning; it examines strengths and opportunities as well as problems; the definition of the problem itself emerges from the data rather than being given in advance; and the act of diagnosing already intervenes in the system by raising awareness and expectations. For these reasons the medical metaphor is deceptive, and OD diagnosis should be understood as a joint inquiry into the current functioning of the whole system.

subjective.question: Describe Lewin's change model.
subjective.answer: Lewin's change model conceives change as a modification of those forces keeping a system's behavior stable, and it has three steps. (1) Unfreezing: creating the motivation to change by disconfirming existing beliefs and behavior, inducing guilt or anxiety about the present state, and providing psychological safety so members can change without loss of identity or integrity. Unfreezing can be personal (directed at individuals), relational, or at system level. (2) Moving: shifting the behavior of the organization, department or individual to a new level — developing new values, attitudes and behaviors through changes in structures and processes, and learning from role models or scanning the environment. (3) Refreezing: stabilizing the organization at the new level by integrating the new behavior into the self-concept (personal refreezing), into significant relationships (relational refreezing), and into the organization's culture, norms, policies and structures (system refreezing), so that the change is sustained.

subjective.question: Name and briefly describe the major data collection methods used in OD diagnosis.
subjective.answer: The major data collection methods are: (1) Questionnaires — survey instruments that collect large amounts of standardized data cheaply and allow quantitative comparison; they are precise and readily available but may lack depth. (2) Interviews — the most widely used data-gathering technique in OD; they obtain rich, in-depth data, including subjective data such as norms, attitudes and values that cannot be observed directly, but they are time-consuming and costly. (3) Observations — watching actual behavior in meetings and work settings; they capture real behavior rather than reported behavior but can be influenced by the observer's presence. (4) Unobtrusive measures — examining records, documents and physical traces without disturbing the system; they are non-reactive but may be incomplete or hard to interpret. There is no one best method; the choice depends on the nature of the problem, and methods are often combined.

subjective.question: What are the characteristics of effective feedback data?
subjective.answer: Effective feedback data should be: relevant to the client; understandable; descriptive rather than evaluative; verifiable, so the client can check their accuracy; timely, fed back soon after collection; limited to a manageable amount; significant, addressing issues the client cares about; comparative, so performance can be judged against some reference; and unfinalized, leaving room for the client to interpret and modify the conclusions during the feedback session.

subjective.question: Briefly describe the five OD practitioner styles.
subjective.answer: The five practitioner styles are: (1) Stabilizer style — the practitioner tries to keep the system running smoothly and avoid rocking the boat; its goal is neither effectiveness nor participant satisfaction. (2) Cheerleader style — emphasis is placed on the satisfaction of organization members and the quality of the work environment, on the assumption that if member satisfaction is high, effectiveness will also be high. (3) Analyzer style — great emphasis is placed on efficiency and expert problem-solving, with little emphasis on member satisfaction; it is based on the belief that the client does not need to know, or cannot learn, the skills to solve its problems. (4) Persuader style — the practitioner focuses on both effectiveness and morale but optimizes neither, often trying to sell a preferred solution. (5) Pathfinder style — the practitioner seeks a high level of both effectiveness and member satisfaction, involving members in diagnosing and solving their own problems. The styles are not mutually exclusive; a practitioner may combine them or move from one style to another as the client's needs change.
